h: פָּרָשַׁת זָכוֹר, מַאֲמָר ד׳ Parshas Zachor — Maamar Daled

p: It is stated in the Gemara (Shabbos 118b):
אִלְמָלֵא שָׁמְרוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל שַׁבָּת רִאשׁוֹנָה כּוּלֵּי
"Had Yisrael kept the first Shabbos," etc.
"And it was on the seventh day" etc.,
and it is written after it, "And Amalek came";
because of the sin concerning keeping Shabbos.
it is stated that because they said,
הֲיֵשׁ ה׳ בְּקִרְבֵּנוּ אִם אָיִן [שְׁמוֹת יז, ז]
and so it is in the holy Zohar
And in the Mechilta (Beshalach, Amalek 1) it is stated:
"Because they slackened their hands from words of Torah,
therefore an enemy came upon them";
And it can be said that all the reasons
is in the secret of Daas
that is, the recognition of His Divinity, Yisbarach,
through joining the wisdom in the mind
with the understanding in the heart,
binding what one grasps with his wisdom
with the will in the heart;
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה בָּא הֶאָרַת אֱלָהוּת לְהַנֶּפֶשׁ
and through this the illumination of Divinity comes to the soul,
from the root, which is the aspect of Keser
and Daas is the inwardness of Keser
(as explained in Parshas Shekalim, beginning of maamar 1);
and the time of the holiness of Shabbos corresponds to it,
opposing the aspect of Daas in holiness;
and he is of one root with Bilam
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק ג רפא, ב)
וְלֹא קָם נָבִיא עוֹד בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמֹשֶׁה
"And there arose no other prophet in Yisrael like Moshe":
"but among the nations one did arise;
and who is this? Bilam," etc.;
וְכֵן הוּא בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (בָּלָק חֵלֶק ג קצג, ב)
and so it is in the holy Zohar (Balak, III 193b).
That is, Bilam was the opposite
of the aspect of Daas of holiness,
he did not want to bind the wisdom in his mind
with the desires of his heart;
for although he grasped in his mind
the preciousness of Yisrael in holiness,
"Let my soul die the death of the upright,"
וְעִם כָּל זֶה הִשִּׂיא עֵצָה לְהַכְשִׁילָם
nevertheless he gave counsel to make them stumble
מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהָיָה לִבּוֹ קָשׁוּר בְּכָל הַתַּאוֹת.
because his heart was bound up in all the lusts.
And this too is the kelipah of Amalek,
who wanted to bring this into Yisrael;
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יֵשׁ שְׁלִיטָה לְהַקְּלִיפּוֹת.
and through this the kelipos have dominion.
had Yisrael kept the first Shabbos,
which is the aspect of Daas in holiness,
Amalek would have had no dominion,
for he is the opponent of this holiness.
וְזֶה גַּם כֵּן עִנְיַן מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ
And this too is the meaning of what they said,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ב סד, ב)
as they said in the holy Zohar (II 64b),
that they wished to know the difference
between Atika, the most Concealed of all concealed,
and Zeir Anpin, which is called Hashem.
That is, they were in doubt
whether the grasp of Divinity is in the aspect of Yesh,
which accords with the intellect of human comprehension,
or in the aspect of Ayin,
And consequently they were not bound in holiness
which is the aspect of Ayin and Atika Kadisha,
And this too is what is meant
by the reason that they slackened their hands from the Torah:
שֶׁהוּא שֶׁכָּל מַעֲשֵׂי הַתּוֹרָה וְהַמִּצְוֹת שֶׁלָּהֶם
namely, that all their deeds of Torah and mitzvos
were done with slackness and laziness,
because they did not bind the wisdom in the mind
with the will in the heart.
It is along the lines of what they said (Berachos 63a):
"Whoever slackens himself from words of Torah
אֵין בּוֹ כֹּחַ לַעֲמוֹד בְּיוֹם צָרָה
has no strength to stand on the day of trouble";
and the Maharsha wrote in Chiddushei Aggados
that even if he learns and fulfills it,
but does so with slackness and in a casual way,
And when one acts with slackness and without strengthening,
הוּא מִפְּנֵי שֶׁחָסֵר מִמֶּנּוּ בְּחִינַת הַדַּעַת
it is because he lacks the aspect of Daas,
which is the strength and the vitality
and the holiness of the Torah and the mitzvos.

paragraphs.text: Shemos Rabbah 26:2 — “What does it say there? 'Is Hashem among us or not?' and 'Amalek came.' What is the connection? It is like a child riding on his father's shoulder who saw his father's friend and asked, 'Have you seen my father?' His father said: 'You are riding on my shoulder and asking about me? I shall put you down, and the enemy will come and rule over you.' So the Holy One said to Israel: 'I carried you upon clouds of glory, yet you say, Is Hashem among us? Therefore the enemy will come and rule over you.' Thus, 'Amalek came.'” The parable describes failure to recognize a sustaining presence already carrying the people. Rav Tzadok joins that loss of recognition to weakened Torah and Shabbos through the unifying quality of daas.

paragraphs.text: Mechilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Amalek 1 — “Others say: Refidim means only slackening of the hands. Because they slackened their hands from words of Torah, the enemy came upon them; the enemy comes only because of slackening from Torah. For it says, 'When Rechavam's kingdom was established and he had grown strong, he abandoned Hashem's Torah, and all Israel with him.' What was the punishment? In Rechavam's fifth year, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem, because they had acted unfaithfully against Hashem.” The Mechilta supports its reading of Refidim with another episode where loss of Torah commitment preceded foreign domination. Rav Tzadok focuses on the inward lack of vitality signified by 'slackening.'

paragraphs.text: Zohar II, Pekudei 221a — “All three are alluded to in this verse: 'In the beginning'—'with wisdom'; 'God created'—'with understanding'; 'the heavens'—'with knowledge.' All three are written in the work of the Mishkan. In this mystery it says: 'These are the accounts of the Mishkan'—the mystery of wisdom; 'the Mishkan of testimony'—the mystery of understanding; 'which was reckoned by Moshe's command'—the mystery of knowledge. Everything corresponds, for whatever the Holy One created in this world He created in the likeness of what is above, and everything is inscribed in the Mishkan's construction.” The Zohar places Moshe at daas within the threefold structure of wisdom, understanding and knowledge. Rav Tzadok explains daas here as the living bond between mental apprehension and the heart's will.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III, Ki Seitzei 281b — “Who is Amalek above? We have seen that the souls of Bilam and Balak came from there; therefore they hated Israel more than any nation or tongue. For this reason Amalek is inscribed in their names: am from Bilam and lak from Balak. They are the male and female Amalekites; of them it is said, 'He has not beheld iniquity in Yaakov, nor seen trouble in Israel.'” The source explicitly relates Bilam and Balak to Amalek's root through their names and hostility. Rav Tzadok identifies their shared inward opposition as the distortion of daas.

paragraphs.text: Sifrei, VeZos HaBerachah, 357:40 — “'No prophet arose again in Israel like Moshe': In Israel none arose, but among the nations one did arise. Who was it? Bilam son of Beor. Yet there is a difference between Moshe's prophecy and Bilam's: Moshe did not know who was speaking with him, while Bilam knew, as it says, 'Who hears God's sayings.' Moshe did not know when He would speak with him until He spoke, while Bilam knew when, as it says, 'Who knows the knowledge of the Most High.' Moshe spoke with Him only standing, as it says, 'Stand here with Me'; Bilam spoke while fallen, as it says, 'Who beholds a vision of the Almighty, fallen and with eyes uncovered.'” The comparison does not erase the differences in prophetic station. The Sifrei continues with the parable of a king's cook who knows the expenses of the royal table; Rav Tzadok uses the comparison as the background for two opposed forms of daas.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III, Balak 193b — “Rabbi Shimon said: Elazar, all the words of wicked Bilam are powerful. The companions explained, 'No prophet arose again in Israel like Moshe': In Israel none arose, but among the nations one arose—Bilam. We have explained the matter: Moshe had no equal among the supernal crowns; Bilam had no equal among the lower crowns. This one belonged to the side of holiness, and that one to the side of the left.” The Zohar expressly makes Moshe and Bilam counterparts in opposing orders. Rav Tzadok explains the contrast ethically as the bond—or refusal to bind—wisdom to the heart's will.

paragraphs.text: Numbers 23:10 — “Who can count Yaakov's dust, or number a fourth part of Israel? May my soul die the death of the upright, and may my end be like theirs.” Bilam's own blessing recognizes Israel's worth and expresses a wish for the end of the upright. Rav Tzadok contrasts that recognition with Bilam's subsequent counsel to corrupt Israel, illustrating wisdom that was not joined to the heart's will.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 106a — “He said to them: 'Their God hates sexual immorality, and they desire linen garments. Come, I shall advise you: Set up enclosures for them, seat prostitutes in them—an old woman outside and a young woman inside—and let them sell linen garments to them.'” This is Bilam's counsel to lead Israel into sin through a staged commercial encounter. Rav Tzadok contrasts the counsel with Bilam's expressed wish to die the death of the upright: intellectual recognition of Israel's value did not govern his will.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Machshavos Charutz 16 — “Bilam and Amalek are joined as one level in evil, for Amalek is the Keser of the kelipah, and Bilam… is its Da’as; Keser and Da’as are one.” There Rav Tzadok adds the holy counterpart: Moshe is the Da’as of holiness, and when he “raised his hand,” lifting Da’as to its root in Keser, the root of Amalek was erased.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Ohr HaChaim on Shemos 17:8 — “Because they grew lax in Torah… and did not engage in the battle of Torah, He punished them with thirst, corresponding to water, and with the fire of Amalek’s war.” The Ohr HaChaim also reads Refidim as laziness in Torah. He adds why Amalek’s war was the fitting consequence: those who failed to wage the “war of Torah” were made to face a war of the sword.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 63a — “Rabbi Tavi said in Rabbi Yoshiyah's name: Whoever slackens himself from words of Torah lacks the strength to stand in a time of trouble, as it says, 'If you slacken on the day of trouble, your strength is narrow.' Rav Ami bar Masna said in Shmuel's name: Even regarding a single commandment, for it says 'You slackened'—in any matter.” The Gemara broadens the danger from Torah to even one mitzvah. Rav Tzadok relates this weakening to action without the inward bond and vitality of daas.

paragraphs.text: Maharsha, Chiddushei Aggados, Berachos 63a, s.v. Kol hamerappeh — “'Whoever slackens himself from words of Torah': Even one who studies and fulfills it—if he does so weakly and as an occasional pursuit, the statement says that he lacks the strength to stand on the day of trouble. As is said in the chapter Ein Omdin: These require strengthening—Torah, good deeds, and so forth; see there.” Maharsha's precision is that the person has not abandoned study and observance; what is deficient is the sustained vigor with which they are pursued. This is the exact distinction Rav Tzadok uses in defining the absence of daas.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 32b — “The Rabbis taught: Four require strengthening: Torah, good deeds, prayer, and worldly occupation. From where do we learn Torah and good deeds? Only be strong and very courageous, to observe and do according to all the Torah: be strong in Torah, and courageous in good deeds. From where prayer? Hope to Hashem; be strong, and let your heart be courageous, and hope to Hashem.” The source names ongoing strengthening as a requirement even for pursuits that are already being practiced. Rav Tzadok treats this vitality as the inward quality whose absence is called slackening.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Tanya, Likkutei Amarim, ch. 3, concluding paragraphs — “Daas denotes attachment and joining: one binds his awareness with a very strong bond and fixes his thought firmly on the greatness of the Infinite One, without turning his attention away. Even someone who wisely understands that greatness will not generate true awe and love in his soul unless he binds his awareness and fixes his thought firmly and continually; otherwise these are empty imaginings. Therefore daas sustains the emotional attributes and gives them life; it embraces kindness and might—that is, love and its branches, and awe and its branches.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Tanya explains the exact missing link diagnosed here: intellectual understanding becomes living love and awe only through sustained attachment. This clarifies why Rav Tzadok describes Torah performed weakly, despite its correct intellectual content, as lacking daas and therefore lacking vitality.
